children: The Trump administration is spending billions of dollars to build U.S. and allied supplies of critical minerals, an effort aimed at reducing China’s leverage over materials essential to defense, technology and manufacturing.

The campaign accelerated after China imposed export controls on seven rare-earth elements and related magnets in April 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday. The restrictions exposed U.S. dependence on China for materials used in products ranging from semiconductors and electric vehicles to missiles and advanced computing systems.

The administration has since mobilized the Defense, Energy, State, Commerce and Interior departments, along with government financing agencies, to support mining, processing and magnet production. The Commerce Department said last year that China was the leading producer of 30 of 44 critical minerals it tracked.

For investors, the effort could create a long-term tailwind for U.S. and allied mining, refining and rare-earth magnet companies. Government financing, purchase commitments and policies favoring non-Chinese supply could improve the economics of projects that previously struggled to compete with lower-cost Chinese production. At the same time, building mines and processing capacity can take years, leaving manufacturers exposed to supply disruptions and volatile mineral prices in the meantime.

U.S. government support has already expanded sharply. The Center for Strategic and International Studies said the response has included billions of dollars in financing, government purchase commitments, price guarantees and partnerships with countries including Australia, Japan, Malaysia and Saudi Arabia.

Washington is also trying to build supply chains with allies rather than relying solely on domestic production. Those efforts come as China continues to wield substantial influence over processing and exports. Recent supply disruptions have shown that dependence remains significant despite U.S. investment.

The challenge is time. Developing mines, refining facilities and magnet plants can take years, and industry experts say fully replacing Chinese supplies is unlikely in the near term. Aerospace companies, for example, are testing alternative materials and recycling programs but still expect China to remain an important supplier for years.

That leaves critical minerals as both an industrial-policy priority and a continuing source of geopolitical risk. For investors, progress in building alternative supply chains could benefit producers outside China, while manufacturers in defense, autos, semiconductors and other industries remain vulnerable to renewed export restrictions or higher input costs.

title: U.S. pours billions into critical minerals push to loosen China’s grip
